headline: Hot Inflation and a Weak Bond Sale Lift Rates
tileReason: Bond markets are closed today for Veterans Day; on Tuesday, hotter-than-expected inflation and a soft 10-year Treasury sale pushed the daily 30-year average up to 7.30% from 7.18%.
takeaway:
Bond markets are closed today for Veterans Day, so today's numbers come from Tuesday, the most recent trading day. On Tuesday the daily 30-year average jumped to 7.30% from 7.18% Monday, its biggest one-day rise in more than a month, though still below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October.

A hotter inflation report set off the jump. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October versus the 0.3% forecasters expected, and core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, closed Tuesday near 4.98%, up about 0.10% from Monday after briefly topping 5%, and the 2-year yield had its biggest one-day jump of the year.

A weak government bond sale added to the pressure. Tuesday afternoon the Treasury sold $42 billion of 10-year notes at a 5.02% yield, a bit above where they were trading just before the sale, with the softest demand since May and the smallest share for overseas and other big investors in over a year. When buyers want a higher return to hold long-term government debt, mortgage rates feel it.

Fed officials sounded more worried about inflation. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger half-point rate hike should be considered in December, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said the Fed needs at least two more quarter-point increases, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the report close to alarming. Futures markets, where traders bet on Fed decisions, now treat a December 9 hike as all but certain, with roughly an 11% chance it is a half point.

Oil bounced back overnight. After two days of steep drops that briefly pushed Brent crude below $90 a barrel Tuesday, Brent was up about 1.6% toward $93 this morning and U.S. crude near $87, after Iran refused to send its enriched nuclear material out of the country and warned of retaliation if attacked again. Treasury futures, which trade even while the cash bond market is closed, suggest the 10-year yield could open above 5% when trading resumes Thursday.

Lenders still have some cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat about 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 9, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%, so lenders have some room to absorb a bond-market selloff. Before Tuesday's jump, the Mortgage Bankers Association's weekly rate fell to 7.21%, its lowest since mid-September, and home loan applications rose about 6%.

The next tests come quickly. Thursday brings a $25 billion 30-year bond sale, weekly jobless claims and Freddie Mac's weekly survey; Friday brings the wholesale inflation report (PPI). After that, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report and the Dec 9 Fed decision are the big ones.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.afterLabel: Late Tue, Nov 10 (bond market closed Wed)
fedOdds.source: The Weekend Spread (Nov 9 close); CME FedWatch via Investing.com and CappNotes (Nov 10); Kalshi and Polymarket via CappNotes (Nov 10); The Blye Sheet (Nov 11)
fedOdds.note: Sources differ a little. CME FedWatch late Tuesday showed about 89% odds of a quarter-point hike and 11% of a half point, so a hike is fully priced. Betting markets Kalshi and Polymarket showed similar odds, with Kalshi still giving about 5% to no change. The Weekend Spread had hike odds near 80% at Monday's close, while CME figures reported Tuesday morning were already about 99% after Waller's remarks.

drivers.title: October inflation runs hotter than forecast
drivers.text: Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October versus 0.3% expected, and core prices (no food or energy) rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected. Higher-than-expected inflation makes bond investors demand higher yields and makes more Fed hikes likely, so the 10-year Treasury yield rose about 0.10% Tuesday to near 4.98%, and lenders raised the daily 30-year average by 0.12% to 7.30%.

drivers.title: Fed officials push for more hikes
drivers.text: Governor Waller said a half-point December hike should be on the table, Dallas Fed President Logan said at least two more quarter-point hikes are needed, and Chicago Fed President Goolsbee called the inflation report close to alarming. Traders now treat a December 9 hike as all but certain, and Goldman Sachs added another hike in March to its forecast. Expectations of higher short-term rates make it harder for mortgage rates to fall.

drivers.title: Soft demand at the 10-year Treasury sale
drivers.text: The $42 billion 10-year sale Tuesday drew the weakest demand since May, and overseas and other big investors took their smallest share in over a year, so the notes sold at 5.02%, slightly above the market level just before. When buyers need a higher yield to absorb all that new debt, the 10-year yield rises and mortgage rates follow. A 30-year bond sale on Thursday is the next test.

drivers.title: Oil rebounds as Iran talks stall
drivers.text: Brent crude briefly fell below $90 a barrel Tuesday for the first time since August, but bounced about 1.6% toward $93 this morning after Iran refused to send its enriched nuclear material abroad and warned of retaliation if attacked. Higher oil feeds into fuel and shipping costs and inflation worries, which tends to push bond yields and mortgage rates up.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.17% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 9, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: lenders can absorb part of a jump in Treasury yields without raising rates as much, and if markets calm down there is room for mortgage rates to improve even if Treasury yields stay put.

outlook.basis: The odds still lean slightly toward higher rates. Inflation has run hotter than forecast two months in a row, a December Fed hike is fully expected with some talk of a larger one, demand at Tuesday's 10-year Treasury sale was soft, and Treasury futures point to the 10-year yield testing 5% when trading resumes Thursday. Some of that is already in Tuesday's jump to 7.30%, though. In borrowers' favor: mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.17% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), which gives lenders room to absorb bond-market swings, and oil is well below its late-October peak. Big swing events: Thursday's 30-year bond sale, Friday's wholesale inflation report, Iran and oil headlines, the Nov 25 report on the Fed's preferred inflation measure, the Dec 4 jobs report and the Dec 9 Fed decision.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average rose to 7.30% Tuesday from 7.18% after a hotter inflation report and a weak Treasury sale, though it's still below the 7.6%-plus levels of early October. Bond markets are closed today, and Treasury futures hint at more pressure when trading resumes Thursday. If you're under contract or close to it, talk with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates turned higher Tuesday after a month of easing, and buyers who waited for a better rate just saw about an eighth of a point come back. A likely December Fed hike could keep rates from falling much further, so realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates jumped to about 7.30% Tuesday after a hot inflation report and a soft Treasury sale, though they're still below early-October highs.
